2611.18585.image_caption: Figure 1: Left: Trident achieves substantially higher reward than EvoTest on Zork1. Right: Trident consistently outperforms baselines across tasks and backbones.

2611.18646.image_caption: Figure 2: The RSIMed training pipeline. Starting from a clinical seed question, the query proposer retrieves medical evidence and the question proposer generates questions with reference answers. A validator checks format and rejects incoherent questions or answers contradicted by newly retrieved evidence. Accepted tasks enter the solver’s pool. Multiple responses receive judge-based rewards for GRPO updates. Solver accuracy and task history guide subsequent difficulty and coverage.

2611.19081.image_caption: Figure 1: Overview of RoboCoEvo. The co-evolution framework of agent and policy improving each other over successive rounds. (a) Policy-Guided Agent Evolution: the agent locates failures in the policy’s failed rollouts and groups recurring failures into failure modes (FMs), shown at the top for each round. For each FM, it writes a detector that identifies the failure state in a rollout (red) and a recovery program that completes the failed subtask from this state in simulation (green). As the policy improves, its rollouts expose FMs that did not occur in earlier rounds. In each subsequent round, the agent writes detectors and recovery programs for the newly identified FMs and refines those of persisting FMs to improve detection accuracy and recovery success. (b) Agent-Guided Policy Capability Expansion: the policy is fine-tuned on the corrective experience together with the original demonstrations, which enables the policy itself to avoid or recover from the targeted failures. The rollouts of the updated policy initiate the next round, and its task success increases over successive rounds. The scores compare the base policy with the policy after RoboCoEvo.

2611.19537.image_caption: Figure 6: A single observation, at step 16,855 of an episode played by the developed program policy in the Troll Mines (floor 5). Top left: the 9 × 11 9\times 11 local map, rendered only from the observation with the Craftax sprites ( Matthews et al. 2024 ) . The outlined cell is the agent, and the dark dotted cells are unlit. Top right: the eight values of each cell, with the sprites that appear in this view and, faded, the other types of the same class. Bottom: the 51 scalars at this step, where the bars show each intrinsic with respect to its maximum.

2611.20430.image_caption: Figure 2: Overview of TrainExplorer, a multi-agent framework for autonomous LLM post-training that integrates strategy planning and execution decoupling. First, strategy planning draws on a structured knowledge base of scientific literature to construct a candidate strategy space. Then, the Idea, Builder, and Critic form an iterative loop for ideation, experimentation, and critique. Within this loop, execution decoupling enables single-component interventions and attributes their effects through controlled comparisons to guide subsequent exploration.

2611.20655.image_caption: Figure 1: From textual lessons to executable constraints. (1) In ScienceWorld, a single irreversible failure reveals an ordering rule: the thermometer must be focused before the target object. (2) Textual self-evolution distills the failure into a correct lesson, but the violating action remains in the candidate set and is still selectable. (3) MetaAct compiles the same rule into a GEAR guard that removes the violating action from the admissible set at execution time: text changes preference, whereas the constraint changes admissibility.

2611.18624.image_caption: Figure 2: Skill Transfer overview. (1) The strong agent runs once under the original skill 𝒮 0 \mathcal{S}_{0} , while the weak agent reruns each iteration under the current skill 𝒮 k \mathcal{S}_{k} on the same training tasks. (2) The Abstractor turns both trajectories into typed node sequences (§ 3.2 ). (3) Aligning the paired structures localizes the gaps on each task and synthesizes the systemic ones into a gap report (§ 3.3 –§ 3.4 ). (4) The patcher edits only the skill, in one pass, to obtain 𝒮 k + 1 \mathcal{S}_{k+1} , which is used to rerun the weak agent. After the iterations, 𝒮 ⋆ \mathcal{S}^{\star} is selected on 𝒱 \mathcal{V} .

2611.18818.image_caption: Figure 3 : Observed gap-weighted surrogate reward versus the change in cumulative bandit-phase practice success rate. Rows show SkillRL, ExpeL, and Shared Reflexion, and columns show ALFWorld and WebShop.

2611.19273.image_caption: Figure 1: Overview of B-OPSD. Student and teacher start from the same base model; the teacher stays frozen while the student is updated. The initial model generates static briefs, while a saved student checkpoint generates refreshed briefs. The current student generates its solution trajectory from the question alone. The frozen teacher receives the question and brief, evaluates the same student prefixes, and provides token-level feedback.

2611.19823.image_caption: Figure 1: Overview of EfficientSkill . From minimal seed 𝒮 0 \mathcal{S}_{0} , Phase 1 repairs failed rollouts on frozen agent ℳ \mathcal{M} without token penalties to discover anchor skill A ∗ A^{*} . Warm-starting from A ∗ A^{*} , Phase 2 prunes episodic output tokens ( E out E_{\text{out}} ) under a ≥ 0.90 ​ A ∗ \geq 0.90\,A^{*} validation gate, yielding concise rules and zero-body-cost workspace tools ( 𝒮 ∗ \mathcal{S}^{*} ).

2611.19901.image_caption: Figure 1 : Learning from past successes and failures for navigation. (a) People recall successful experiences and mistakes to guide navigation. (b) Similar visual cues may cause an agent to confuse a kitchen with a laundry room; replaying a past failure helps correct this mistake. Inspired by episodic memory, R 2 A reuses successful and failed experiences with outcome feedback for adaptation.

2611.19952.image_caption: Figure 5: Continuing-service pilot. Left: a retained camera observation from the fixed-pelvis R1 tabletop scene. Right: accepted completions over all 20 scored assignments in each paired stream. Streams 0–2 have fixed requirements; streams 3–5 change requirement. Object layouts vary, and external setup is logged between jobs. This is a six-pair simulation pilot using one push skill.

2611.20759.image_caption: Figure 1: (a) CLAM overview: sessions are consolidated into a carried workspace Q t Q_{t} via a recurrent hypernetwork that decodes Q N Q_{N} into a LoRA adapter; the episodic buffer retrieves spans at query time. (b) One consolidation step: Q t − 1 Q_{t-1} cross-attends into session activations Z t Z_{t} , slots reorganise via self-attention, and a gate controls the write.

2611.21019.image_caption: Figure 1: Memory errors pass as valid evidence, so an answer built on a faulty record looks grounded yet is wrong (A). They propagate to the later questions that read the same record (B). Since the same wrong answer can stem from writing, updating or answering, an error must be attributed to the stage where it began before it can be repaired (C).

2611.21115.image_caption: Figure 1 : Overview of ReuseMem. The robot records case contents and origins before later requests are known. The same memory supplies different historical evidence for each goal, while current observations guide the next manipulation.

2611.19700.image_caption: Figure 2 : One round on a task. (1) The adaptation mechanism receives a task. (2) Prepare returns a context c c , with which the agent makes k k attempts y i y_{i} in fresh sessions of the environment. (3) Observe receives the attempts and their outcomes o i o_{i} and updates the mechanism’s non-parametric state. (4) TeacherContexts adds hindsight h h for SDPO’s self-teacher. (5) The mechanism updates its parametric state using the weighted SDPO and GRPO losses.

2611.20873.image_caption: Fig. 7: Median tokens per episode by task type and primary model, as routed during the trace.

2611.21449.image_caption: Figure 1: First-layer weight norms per input channel for the four original games. Each map is the 10 × \times 10 grid; a cell’s colour is the size of the 32 weights leaving that input, scaled independently from the minimum (palest) to the maximum (darkest) weight for each input channel for each game. The bottom row is the Breakout network with its weights shuffled, as in the original MIT control.
